content.title: About
content.content: Tempura is a Japanese dish where pieces of fish, tofu and assorted vegetables are coated in a light batter and quickly deep‑fried. The cooking method preserves the natural flavors of the ingredients while the crisp crust adds a pleasant texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tempura was introduced to Japan in the 16th century by Portuguese missionaries.
The traditional batter is made from cold water and flour without leavening agents, resulting in a delicate, airy coating.
Common fish used include white fish such as snapper or salmon, which pair well with tofu that absorbs the batter’s flavor.
Vegetables are usually sliced thinly or cut into bite‑size pieces to ensure rapid cooking.
Tempura is often served with a dipping sauce made from dashi, mirin and soy sauce, sometimes enhanced with grated daikon.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Fish and tofu provide complete protein essential for muscle maintenance and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Fatty fish such as salmon contain omega‑3s that support heart and brain health.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Vegetables in tempura (e.g., carrots, bell peppers, broccoli) are rich in vitamins A, C and potassium.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Tempura contains no added sugars, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: Brief frying retains most nutrients while the light crust is gentle on the digestive system.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Because it is deep‑fried, tempura can be calorie‑dense and contain saturated fats.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to fish or shellfish should avoid this dish.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Dipping sauces are often salty; moderation is advised.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: Overheating oil (above 180 °C) can produce acrylamides; keep frying temperature around 170‑180 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve tempura hot, dipping each piece in tempura sauce or soy sauce with grated ginger. A squeeze of lemon or a side of grated daikon adds freshness. It pairs well with steamed rice or a light salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Tempura is best enjoyed immediately. Leftovers can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days, though the crust will lose its crunch. Reheat in a 180 °C oven for 5‑7 minutes to restore texture.
